subject: Medicine
summary: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by chronic venous hypertension and valve incompetence. They are common, especially in women, and can progress to chronic venous insufficiency.

sections.p: Varicose veins are visibly enlarged superficial veins, usually in the legs, diagnosed by clinical inspection and duplex ultrasound confirming reflux.

t.b: Does the vein have reflux? → Confirms venous insufficiency; normal flow rules out significant reflux.

sections.p: The CEAP classification grades clinical severity from C0 (no signs) to C6 (active ulcer). Staging guides treatment intensity.
Chronic venous hypertension from valve failure is primary; secondary causes increase pressure or damage valves.
b: Pelvic congestion (e.g., from pregnancy or portal hypertension)
Infections (e.g., lymphatic filariasis) in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Patients notice bulging, blue‑purple veins, heaviness, aching, and sometimes swelling after prolonged standing.
Focused imaging and labs identify reflux, rule out DVT, and detect contributing systemic disease.

t.b: Is there reflux or obstruction? → Positive reflux confirms diagnosis; no reflux suggests other causes.
Is arterial disease present? → Low ABI (<0.9) contraindicates compression therapy.
Is there infection or inflammation? → Elevated markers may indicate cellulitis or thrombophlebitis.

sections.p: Complications include chronic venous insufficiency, ulceration, superficial thrombophlebitis, and rare bleeding.
Treat underlying cause, use compression, and consider procedural correction when symptoms are moderate‑severe.
b: Compression stockings (30‑40 mmHg) to reduce venous pressure
Endovenous laser/ radiofrequency ablation for refluxing truncal veins

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, skin, and ulcer healing; reinforce lifestyle measures to prevent progression.
b: Encourage weight control, activity, and avoidance of prolonged standing

sections.p: Conditions that mimic varicose veins may be mistaken for them.
b: Deep vein thrombosis (painful, swollen, not visible veins)

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or alarming.
b: Normal duplex does not exclude early reflux; repeat if symptoms persist
Compression may mask edema, hiding early skin changes

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden leg pain with warmth and swelling (possible DVT)
New ulcer or bleeding from a vein
Rapid increase in swelling or discoloration

faq.q: Can varicose veins cause blood clots?
faq.a: They rarely cause embolic events, but superficial thrombophlebitis can occur and should be treated.
No; many patients improve with compression and lifestyle changes; procedures are reserved for persistent symptoms or complications.

faq.q: Do pregnancy‑related varicose veins resolve after delivery?
faq.a: Often they improve, but some women retain veins and may need later treatment.

exam: Describe the CEAP classification and its clinical relevance.
Explain how duplex ultrasound differentiates varicose veins from deep vein thrombosis.
Outline the stepwise management of a patient with symptomatic C3 varicose veins.
